rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
P=1/f with f in metres; 1 D=1 m⁻¹.
Contact thin lenses: Peq=ΣPi and feq=1/Peq.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Lens Power Definition:** Power $P = 1/f$ (in meters) measured in diopters (D). A converging lens has $P > 0$, a diverging lens has $P < 0$. Power is additive for thin lenses in contact: $P_{total} = \sum P_i$.  ·  **Combination of Thin Lenses:** For thin lenses in contact, the total focal length is given by $1/f_{total} = \sum 1/f_i$, or equivalently $P_{total} = \sum P_i$. This assumes negligible separation between lenses. For separated lenses, use the equivalent focal length formula including the separation $d$.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Using centimetres directly produces a power 100 times too large.  ·  Separated or thick lens systems require an additional relation.

rows.text: f=+0.25 m gives +4 D; f=−0.50 m gives −2 D.  ·  +4 D and −1.5 D in contact give +2.5 D, feq=0.40 m.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres. Opticians add powers because two thin lenses in contact really do add. A +2.0 D lens and a −0.50 D lens in contact give +1.5 D, a weaker converging pair.  ·  The working relations are P = 1/f with f in metres and Powers in contact add. Name each symbol, convert the data into SI units, and only then substitute.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Lens power measures convergence or divergence: P=1/f when f is in metres. Its SI-derived unit is the dioptre, 1 D=1 m⁻¹. A converging lens has positive power and a diverging lens negative power in air.  ·  Worked example: f=+25 cm=+0.25 m gives P=+4 D. A diverging lens with f=−50 cm=−0.50 m has P=−2 D.  ·  Thin lenses in contact have additive powers. A +4 D lens and −1.5 D lens make Peq=+2.5 D, so feq=1/2.5=0.40 m.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Worked case  ·  **Power vs Magnification:** Lens power $P = 1/f$ relates to focal length, not directly to magnification. Magnification $m = v/u = f/(f-u)$ depends on object distance. A high-power lens (short $f$) gives larger magnification for a given object distance, but $m$ is not simply proportional to $P$.  ·  A vector answer needs a direction as well as a magnitude.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A special case, such as a right angle or a steady temperature, has to be stated before it is used.  ·  Find the focal length of a +1.5 D combination, and the focal length of the +2.0 D lens alone.  ·  Power is not magnification: focal length determines power, while image size and orientation also depend on object distance through the lens equation.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: For separated lenses the equivalent power includes separation; the simple algebraic sum applies only when thin lenses are in contact or separation is negligible.
